newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir's Abdullah returns to walk tightrope.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir's Abdullah returns to walk tightrope.

text.p: Farooq Abdullah, set to become chief minister of India's strife-torn Jammu and Kashmir state, is returning from the political wilderness to walk a tightrope between separatists and federal politicians in New Delhi.
His National Conference party emphatically won last month's state elections, results showed on Wednesday.
But there are many in Kashmir who say the 62-year-old leader failed the test during two previous tenures as chief minister.

"He cannot solve anything," said lawyer and separatist leader Pir Hafizullah Makhdoomi, who argued that Farooq's party had alienated many former supporters. "He has come into the political process only to save his own party."

The British-trained doctor with a taste for the high life was last elected chief minister in 1987 in a controversial poll alliance with India's Congress party, which many Kashmiris say sowed the seeds of a rebellion in 1990.
Abdullah was accused by rivals of rigging the elections, which critics say forced rivals to support separatism.
"In a way he is responsible for militancy, because this led his rivals to become separatists or militants," a shopkeeper in the state's summer capital Srinagar said.
"But this time, voters had no option. The National Conference is the only truly Kashmiri party."

New Delhi dismissed Abdullah's government in 1990, saying he was soft on rebels, and deployed tens of thousands of soldiers and paramilitary troops. Since then, police and hospital sources estimate 20,000 people have died in the violence.
Despite widespread disenchantment with his rule, Abdullah remains a towering leader in the state, thanks mainly to his father, Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah.

For most Kashmiris, Farooq Abdullah still wears the mantle and carries the credibility of his father, the "Lion of Kashmir", who dominated regional politics for half a century, much of it from jail, before dying in 1982.
"There is a major responsibility on me and my party to deliver the goods," Abdullah told Reuters on Wednesday.
The National Conference stayed out of general elections in May, saying the federal government, then led by Congress, was not seriously committed to granting Kashmir greater autonomy.
But Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition pledged "maxiumum autonomy" after assuming power in June.
Abdullah has said he wants the restoration of powers which before 1952 lay in the state's hands but which have since been seized by the federal government.
The Indian constitution gives the state nominal charge of all areas but communications, defence and foreign relations.
The constitution also gave the state the right to select its own Sadar-e-Riyasat, or president, who could not be dismissed by New Delhi without the state government's consent.
"Disco Farooq", whose wife is English, has a penchant for night life and spent much of the past six years in London, stirring animosity among some Kashmiris.
Many Kashmiri villagers remember him for driving a famous Indian film star on a scooter along the hilly roads of the Pahalgam holiday resort in the early 1980s.

He also has a tough streak. Recently he said separatists "must be made to suffer". On Wednesday he pledged to crack down on armed militants. But he also held out an olive branch to unarmed separatists, saying he hoped for talks with them.
